definition: A security technique that converts passwords into fixed-length strings of characters using mathematical algorithms, making it nearly impossible to reverse the process and recover the original password.
metaDescription: Password hashing protects your passwords by converting them into irreversible codes. Learn how this security technique keeps your accounts safe.
simpleExplanation: Instead of storing your actual password, websites use a special mathematical process to scramble it into a random-looking code. Even if hackers steal this code, they can't easily figure out what your original password was.
whyItMatters: Password hashing protects you when data breaches occur. Without it, hackers could immediately see everyone's passwords in plain text. With hashing, your actual password remains hidden even if the company's database is compromised.
technicalDetail: Hashing uses one-way cryptographic functions like bcrypt, scrypt, or Argon2 to transform passwords. Good hashing includes 'salting' (adding random data) and multiple rounds of processing to resist brute-force attacks. Modern algorithms are deliberately slow to make cracking attempts computationally expensive.

examples.explanation: When you create a password 'MySecret123', the website converts it to something like '$2b$12$LQv3c1yqBWVHxkd0LQ4YCOuLQv3c1y' and stores only this hashed version.
If a company's password database is stolen, attackers see only scrambled hashes instead of actual passwords, making it extremely difficult to access user accounts.
When you log in, the system hashes your entered password and compares it to the stored hash rather than comparing plain text passwords.
